subtopic_detail: Croup severity assessment and dexamethasone dosing
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in a metropolitan emergency department. A 2 year old boy is brought in by his mother at 2 am with a 1 day history of a barking cough and a hoarse voice.

On arrival he is alert and consolable in his mother's arms. He has a barking cough but no stridor when calm. Stridor becomes audible when he cries during examination. There is mild suprasternal recession only when upset, no tracheal tug at rest, and air entry is equal with no wheeze. He has taken a small amount of oral fluid in the last hour.

Pulse rate 128/min, blood pressure 100/60 mmHg, respiratory rate 32/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 37.6 degrees C. His immunisations are up to date.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 128/min; BP 100/60 mmHg; RR 32/min; SpO2 98% RA; T 37.6 C
data_table.Examination: Alert; barking cough; hoarse voice; stridor only when crying; mild suprasternal recession when upset; air entry equal; no wheeze
data_table.History: 1 day symptoms; immunisations up to date; taking small oral fluids

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial pharmacological treatment?

options.text: Oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg as a single dose, and discharge home once settled and tolerating fluids
options.rationale: This child has mild croup: stridor only when upset, no stridor at rest, no significant recession at rest. Oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg once is first line for mild and moderate croup and discharge is safe once the child is settled and taking fluids (Source: RCH CPG: Croup; TG Respiratory).
